title: The Night of Power
hookLine: the Quran calls one night in Ramadan better than a thousand months (Quran 97)

lines: A HANDFUL OF NIGHTS KEEP THEIR SHAPE.
cards: Some nights you remember for the rest of your life. The night someone was born. The night you got the call.
The night you stayed up talking until the sky went gray. Most of the calendar blurs, but a handful of nights keep their shape. Now take that as far as it goes.
What if one single night were worth more than years of ordinary ones? The Quran says exactly that about one night, in a short chapter that opens the nights of wonder closing this block on awe.
Its name is the Night of Power.

teach.h: WE REVEALED IT ON THE NIGHT OF POWER.
teach.b: First, what the chapter says happened. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power."
Muslim tradition understands this as the Quran itself: the night, tradition says, when its revelation began, in the month of Ramadan.
Then the chapter asks a question, as if even the listener can't quite take it in: "Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is!" Second, the comparison.
"The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." Not equal to. Better than.
Tradition hears in it that worship and good done on that one night outweigh a very long stretch of ordinary time. Third, what fills the night.
The chapter says the angels and the Spirit come down that night, by the permission of their Lord.
And the chapter ends on a single word of mood: "Peace until the rising of the dawn." Not a night of thunder, but of descent and peace, all the way to morning. Fourth, how Muslims keep it.
The chapter doesn't name the date.
Tradition, from the hadith, says to seek it in the last nights of Ramadan, so those nights are kept with extra prayer, reading the Quran and asking forgiveness, some people staying in the mosque.
Part of the awe is in not knowing exactly which night it is. So people stay awake for several, treating each one as if it might be the one.

how: Muslim tradition seeks Laylat al-Qadr in the last nights of Ramadan, kept with extra prayer, Quran recitation and asking forgiveness; some stay in the mosque for those final days and nights.

o: the angel who brings the Quran down to earth
the last night of Ramadan, when the fast is broken
power or decree, the name of the night revelation began

p: when, tradition says, the Quran came down
what the night is better than

s: the chapter says the Night of Power is equal to a thousand months
"better than a thousand months": not equal to, better than.
the chapter pauses to ask what the Night of Power is
"Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is!"
the chapter ends with peace until dawn
"Peace until the rising of the dawn."

games.q: the chapter has just said: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power." what comes next?
o: a question: what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is!
a warning about the day of judgment.
games.why: the chapter pauses on a question, as if the night is too large to take in at once, then answers: better than a thousand months.

practice: Sit as if it were late: lights low if you can, the house still, shoulders dropped. Hold the chapter's last words, peace until the rising of the dawn, and let them set the pace of your breath.
If you pray, this quiet can be prayer; if you don't, keep it as a small piece of night worth remembering.

wordCard.voice: al-Qadr. The Power, or Decree, named in the night when Muslim tradition says the Quran began to come down: angels, peace, and morning. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Night of Power, also translated the Night of Decree; the name of the night in Surah 97.

carryVoice: Your line: better than a thousand months. One night, weighed against years. That closes the week.
